subject: [PATCH RFC] mm/gup: batch contiguous pages in follow_page_mask() and return them via a pages array

reviews.author: Lorenzo (ARM)
reviews.summary:
Reviewer Lorenzo expressed concerns about the patch's readability and maintainability, specifically citing excessive use of walls of text, redundant code comments, and lack of refactoring to improve technical debt.

Reviewer Lorenzo (ARM) expressed disagreement with the patch, citing concerns about the quality of code generated by fable, a tool used in the submission process, and suggested using it as guidance only rather than implementing its suggestions directly.

Reviewer Lorenzo expressed strong disagreement with the patch, citing reviewer/submitter asymmetry and AI slop as major concerns, which he believes will lead to rejection of similar submissions in the future.
reviews.raw_body:
Thanks for doing a human pass but it LLM's habits really carried through
here. In general:

- No walls of text please - fewer words are better, clarity is king.

- Don't write the code in English as a comment/commit msg - redudant and
  distracting.

- Sensible patch separation obviously please.

- Write as elegant/reasonable code as possible. If the code you touch was
  some horrible mega-function, take the time to refactor it. Pay down
  technical debt.

These are all things LLMs are extremely bad at (even fable). So they need
to be done by a human.

---

Unfortunately based on your recent submissions I don't agree.

In general, even with fable, I've found that the code it generates is
nowhere near kernel quality.

I'd suggest using the generated code as guidance only and the LLM for
checking things rather than making things.

---

Well as you can tell I'm not afraid to - well I wouldn't say yell, more
civilised than that - protest :)

In general, again, the human layer is what's needed here not more rules
IMO.

Reviewer/submitter asymmetry was already a huge problem, AI slop makes it
critical and means people repeatedly submitting things that look like that
will get rejected out of hand.

Let's try to avoid that here :)

reviews.author: Rik Riel (author)
reviews.summary:
The author is addressing a concern about the patch's adherence to kernel coding style rules and its readability, specifically regarding the use of comments and formatting. The author acknowledges that the code may not be perfect but explains that they are working on building a collection of kernel-style rules in a separate repository and plans to address these issues in future revisions.

Author acknowledges the importance of improving tooling and agrees that AI-generated code can be a better starting point, but notes that human judgment is still necessary.
sentiment_signals: acknowledges the value of AI-generated code
emphasizes the need for human judgment
reviews.raw_body:
LLMs can apply those rules, when expressed in a way
that they get interpreted unambiguously by the LLM.

I'm slowly building up a collection of such rules
in the kernel-style repository.

AI can write in any style you ask it to.

/*
 * Long in the Halls of Rq the weary wait,                   
 * till __schedule, herald of the turning years,             
 * calls forth the next to walk the road of fate             
 * as prev fades west.                
 */      

AI can also flag such issues, once it knows to
look for them.

---

The 80/20 rule comes into play here.

If AI produces junk, the person starting with
LLM-produced code can spend days cleaning it
up, without getting things in a reasonable state.

If the AI produces a better starting point, the 
remaining issues will stand out like a sore thumb, 
and it's much easier to find and fix them.

I agree there will always be a need for human
judgment, but that doesn't mean we should not
improve our tooling.


-- 
All Rights Reversed.

2026-08-01.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the way Linux handles page table walks by batching contiguous pages in the follow_page_mask() function and returning them via a pages array. This reduces the number of repeated page table walks, especially for PTE-mapped large folios, which can lead to significant performance improvements. The patch also simplifies the code by removing unnecessary loops and refactoring the logic to avoid restarting the walk at every folio boundary. Additionally, it fixes a silent correction in the old page_increm clamp, making it more robust and reliable.

reviews.author: David (Arm)
reviews.summary:
Reviewer David expressed frustration about the increasing use of LLMs in code reviews, suggesting that such exercises should be done privately and not burden reviewers with sifting through generated comments.

Reviewer David (Arm) expressed frustration that others are not contributing their own code and instead relying on the patch author's work, stating it is unacceptable and that they will start ignoring such behavior.
reviews.raw_body:
Just the important note that people can use LLMs to make themselves
more efficient (if they think so), but not by delegating the hard work
of sifting through slop (code and/or comments) to the poor souls that have
to review it.

LLM exercises should be done behind closed curtains without us noticing.

---

Right. But what happens instead is that people think it's okay to not do
that work and instead workslop us.

That is simply not acceptable, and we'll have to start ignoring people
where this is a recurring theme. We simply don't have the time to do other
peoples work.

-- 
Cheers,

David

reviews.author: Lorenzo (ARM)
reviews.summary: Reviewer Lorenzo (ARM) expressed frustration that the patch, although addressing a specific issue, adds to the reviewer's workload and may be ignored if not carefully reviewed.
sentiment_signals: reviewer's tone is more about process than technical concerns
reviews.raw_body:
Yes exactly, this is the problem and this patch was a prime example of it.

The theme here is 'please don't add to the impossible review load' or you will
receive a >/dev/null resolution to the problem :)
